units.translation: Thus Hermann corrected what is in M: ἐπιδρομω [rushing upon] (with ο written over ω) ποθι θάνατος ὅπηι [wherever death is], on which the scholiast noted: ὅπου θάνατος ἀπῇ, ἐκεῖ τῶν ἀνθρώπων εὐπραγούντων τιμαὶ τοῖς θεοῖς ἐπιτρέχουσιν [where death is absent, there, when men prosper, honors run to the gods]. Hermann rightly wrote ἐπίδρομ᾽ ὁπόθι [rushing upon wherever], but for ἀπῇ [is absent] undoubtedly ἐπῇ [is present] should be written with Weil.
And to the gods, pure offerings, when things go well, rush upon wherever death is absent.
where death is absent, there, when men prosper, honors run to the gods
I join. Of yoking horses to a chariot.
Having yoked this chariot to horses in their prime.
Nor may your mouth be yoked to evil reports.
to be emulated, to be envied. Of one who is proclaimed blessed.
But he who is not begrudged is not enviable.

Thus rightly Schütz for κἀπιθοάζουσ᾽ [and crying aloud] (οα in an erasure in M). The same fault of the manuscripts is in Euripides Med. 1409 τάδε καὶ θρηνώ κἀπιθεάζω μαρτυρόμενος δαίμονας [these things I lament and call upon the gods, calling the divinities to witness]. Hesychius: ἐπιθεάζει: θεοὺς ἐπικαλεῖται [he calls upon the gods]. For examples of this form and of the other ἐπιθειάζω [to call upon the gods] see Thes. vol. 3 p. 1598.
Praying these things and calling upon the gods.
these things I lament and call upon the gods, calling the divinities to witness
And it is lawful to desire with excessive passion the blood of a virgin.
He paid this full penalty, sacrificing upon fresh offerings.
I shout to, I incite by shouting.
Indeed I will command and shout to you.
Did you not hear when you shouted this?

Thus Stephanus wrote for μὴ πικαινόντων [not making new], which is in M, or μὴ ἐπικαινόντων [not making new], which is in the copies. More probably μὴ πικραινόντων [not embittering] Valckenaer in Thes. vol. 6 p. 1075 or μὴ ἐπιχραινόντων [not touching] Wakefield.
When the citizens themselves do not make new laws.

I invoke. From this form is derived the aorist with reduplication ἐκεκλόμην, whose third person is ἐκέκλετο and ἐπεκέκλετο, and the participle κεκλόμενος (or ἐπικεκλόμενος) was used by the epic poets, after whose example Aeschylus spoke.
Calling upon the heifer of Zeus.
For I will not conceal you (σ᾽ added by Musgrave).
i.e. proclaimed king of the land.
Having mounted the towers and been proclaimed to the city
O child of Zeus, he is thievish.
I spin the threads of fate, I destine.
For this lot the piercing Fate spun to hold steadfastly.
And upon her children she sent wrathful curses.
